- **Source ID:** `assh-dupuytrens-contracture`
- **URL:** https://www.assh.org/handcare/condition/dupuytrens-contracture
- **Author:** American Society for Surgery of the Hand
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/assh-dupuytrens-contracture.txt`
- **Main subjects:** what Dupuytren's contracture is and how it forms, who is affected and the known risk factors, how the disease is noticed, evaluated, and staged, nonsurgical treatment options and their recurrence rates, surgical treatment options and recovery
- **Anatomy:** palmar fascia, cords, nodules, ring finger, little finger, knuckles, soles of the feet, genital tissue
- **Management options:** observation for mild cases, splinting or stretching (not preventive, but safe), needle fasciotomy (needle aponeurotomy), collagenase injection, surgical fasciotomy, surgical fasciectomy, post-treatment splinting and hand therapy
- **Important concepts:** fascia thickening into non-contractile cord tissue, Dupuytren's diathesis, the tabletop test, recurrence versus cure

**A cord running from the palm into a finger, pulling it toward the palm** `[p.1]`.
**Inability to lay the hand flat on a table, or open it fully** `[p.2]`.
**Difficulty washing hands, wearing gloves, holding large objects, using pockets, or shaking hands** `[p.2]`.
**Lumps on the soles of the feet, or thickening on the knuckles, alongside hand symptoms** `[p.2]`.

**Retreatment need**, tracked as a downstream consequence of progression `[¶6]`.
**Recurrence of contracture in the originally treated digit** `[¶6]`.
**New Dupuytren's intervention needed in a digit that was not initially treated**, whether in the same hand or the opposite one `[¶6]`.
**Pre-existing, untreated contracture in a digit other than the one initially addressed**, named repeatedly as a risk factor for further treatment regardless of location `[¶6]`.
**Firm nodules fixed to the skin or deep fascia, with skin thickening or pitting in the palm** `[p.1]`.
**Fibrous, tendon-like cords, and flexion deformity at the MCPJ and IPJ** `[p.1]`.
**Reduced span between thumb and index finger webspace; inability to lay the palm flat on a table** `[p.1]`.
**Ectopic nodules over the dorsal PIPJs, soles of the feet, or penile tissue** `[p.1]`.
**Persistent painful nodules**, distinguished in the pathway from nodules that are simply present but not painful `[p.1]`.
**Difficulty extending the fingers, from a fibrous cord in the palm or finger** `[¶2]`.

**Recurrence of contracture after initial successful treatment**, defined explicitly per study rather than left to inconsistent wording `[¶5]`.
**Need for a repeat procedure (reintervention)** as a distinct, trackable consequence of recurrence `[¶6]`.

sections.body:
**Dupuytren's contracture is fascia in the palm turning into thickened, static cord tissue that can pull the
fingers into a bent position — it is not curable, and every current treatment removes or breaks the cord
without preventing it from coming back.** `[p.1]`, `[p.2]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[p.1]`

**Fascia is the fibrous tissue that normally covers nerves, blood vessels, muscles, and tendons in the hand,
and stabilizes the skin.** In Dupuytren's disease, "this fascia can become abnormal. It becomes thicker,
forming cords." The source is explicit about what distinguishes a cord from a tendon: "Unlike a tendon that
is moved by a muscle that shortens and lengthens, cord tissue is not connected to a muscle. Cord tissue is
static and does not move."

**There may be one cord or several, separate or connected**, and most people also develop **nodules or
bumps** in the hand. Course is unpredictable: "these nodules and cords may not change for a long time. They
can also have a slow or fast change."
sections.heading: What it is

sections.body:
`[p.1]`

The source states the cause plainly as unresolved: **"The exact cause of Dupuytren's contracture is unknown
and very complex."** What is stated as known:

- **It is a hereditary disease** — "family history and ancestry play a role."
- **More common** in men, people over age 40, and people of Northern European descent.
- **Less common** in African and Middle Eastern descent.
- **Related**: smoking, diabetes, alcohol, lower body mass index, and aging.
- **Not related**: "There is no evidence that hand injuries or specific jobs lead to a higher risk of
  developing Dupuytren's contracture." A mild relationship to trauma is allowed only for someone already at
  risk, and occasionally "after a distal radius (wrist) fracture, a patient may develop a single nodule in
  the palm" that "often does not progress to result in a bent finger joint."
sections.heading: Who is affected

sections.body:
`[p.1]`–`[p.2]`

Symptoms are **"lumps, nodules, and bands or cords on the palmar side of the hands,"** firm and stuck to the
skin, with the skin itself often thicker and puckered. The source's own analogy for this: **"Think of the
Dupuytren's palm skin like a road. Some areas are swollen and puffy like a speed bump. In other areas the
skin is puckered and pulled down like a pothole."**

**The ring finger and little finger are most commonly involved**, either hand can be affected, and each hand
can progress on its own pattern and timeline. **It is usually not painful**, though lumps can be uncomfortable
in some people. It's often first noticed as **difficulty placing the hand flat on a surface** (the tabletop
test, Figure 3) or opening the hand fully — with downstream effects on washing hands, wearing gloves, holding
large objects, using pockets, and (if the right hand is involved) shaking hands.

**Severity is hard to predict**, but the source names concrete risk markers: earlier age of onset predicts
more severe disease; men develop more severe symptoms than women; more affected relatives predicts higher
risk; and involvement elsewhere in the body — **"called Dupuytren's diathesis"** — also predicts higher risk.
That elsewhere-involvement can appear as **plantar fibromatosis** (soles of the feet), **Peyronie's disease**
(the genital location, in men), or a **knuckle pad (or Garrod's pad)** on top of the knuckles.
sections.heading: How it's noticed and how severe it gets

sections.body:
`[p.2]`

**Not every palm lump is Dupuytren's**, so the source recommends a hand surgeon examination. "Sometimes a
history and examination is all that is needed," and imaging (x-ray, ultrasound, or MRI) is used at other
times. Factors weighed: **size, "feel," location, presence of pain, movement of the mass or skin around it,
family history, and other medical conditions.**
sections.heading: Evaluation

sections.body:
`[p.2]`–`[p.3]`

Two office-based options, both described as *reducing* the cord rather than removing it:

| Option | What happens | Recovery | Recurrence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Needle fasciotomy (needle aponeurotomy)** | Local numbing, then a needle cuts the cord in several places below the skin; the hand is then slowly stretched to break the cord | "Only a few days" | **"Roughly one third of patients will see the cord eventually come back after this procedure"** |
| **Collagenase injection** | Two visits: an injectable drug dissolves the cord at visit one; at visit two the numbed hand is stretched to break the cord | "Only a few days to a few weeks" | **"One third of patients will see the cord come back"** |

Both can cause small skin tears that heal over a few weeks, and both are explicitly stated to **not remove
the cord fully from below the skin** — which the source ties directly to the recurrence figure it gives for
each. Splinting and therapy may follow either, aimed at keeping the hand straight and rebuilding the ability
to make a fist.
sections.heading: Nonsurgical treatment

sections.body:
`[p.3]`

Two procedures, distinguished by how much tissue is removed:

- **Fasciotomy** — the tight cords are cut but not removed. "This is less invasive as only a small cut or
  cuts are used," but **"because all the tissue is not removed, there is possibly a higher chance the
  contracture could return."**
- **Fasciectomy** — cuts the cords *and* removes as much of the nodule, cords, and diseased skin as needed.
  "This often has longer wounds with more extensive dissection."

Surgery is outpatient/same-day, under a variety of anesthesia approaches, with either stitched or
intentionally-open wounds to reduce recurrence risk. **Fasciectomy recovery is about 6 weeks**, with hand use
continuing during that time, and the source frames post-surgical effort as directly determining outcome:
**"The more the patient does soon after surgery, the more successful the final result will be."** Waiting too
long to start therapy "may result in stiffness."

sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Cord** — thickened, non-contractile fascia; "not connected to a muscle... static and does not move" `[p.1]`.
- **Dupuytren's diathesis** — a pattern of disease appearing elsewhere in the body (feet, genitals, knuckles)
  alongside the hand, associated with more severe disease `[p.2]`.
- **Needle fasciotomy / needle aponeurotomy** — an in-office needle procedure that cuts the cord without
  removing it `[p.2]`.
- **Fasciectomy** — surgical removal of the cord, nodule, and affected skin, as distinct from a fasciotomy
  that only cuts the cord `[p.3]`.

sections.body:
This is a patient-education handout from a professional hand-surgery society, not a study — its hedges are
plain-language limits on certainty rather than statistical caveats, and they are preserved here rather than
smoothed into confidence the source does not claim:

- **Cause: "unknown and very complex"** `[p.1]`.
- **Course: "It is difficult to predict how the disease will progress"** `[p.2]`.
- **Cure: "Even with treatment, the disease is not fully curable. The nodules and cords may come back in the
  same or a different location"** `[p.2]`.
- **Both nonsurgical options are stated with a specific, matching recurrence figure (roughly one third)**,
  and both are explicitly described as not removing the cord fully `[p.2]`–`[p.3]`.
- **Surgical improvement is stated as not guaranteed to last**: "this improvement may not maintained forever"
  [sic in source] `[p.3]`.
- **Splinting/stretching is explicitly stated as non-preventive**: "typically does not prevent worsening of
  the contracture but is safe to try" `[p.2]`.

sections.body:
**In a randomized trial of 302 patients, surgery produced significantly less progression in the treated
finger than either needle fasciotomy or collagenase injection over 2 years — but none of the treatments
changed how likely progression was in fingers that weren't treated** `[¶6]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶5]`

This is a **finger-level analysis from the DETECT (Dupuytren Treatment Effectiveness Trial) dataset**,
covering **302 participants and 423 initially treated fingers**. Progression was defined precisely, not left
to judgment: **"an increase in contracture angle between 3 months and 2 years after treatment."** The
analysis deliberately separates three finger categories — the treated finger itself, an adjacent untreated
finger, and all untreated fingers — to see whether treating one finger has any spillover effect on others.
sections.heading: The trial design

sections.body:
`[¶6]`

Follow-up was strong: **279 of 302 participants (92%) completed 3-month measurements, and 274 (91%) completed
2-year measurements.** In treated fingers, **surgery resulted in significantly less progression than needle
fasciotomy** (mean difference 9.7°, 95% CI 3.7 to 16°) **and less than collagenase injection** (mean
difference 6.0°, 95% CI 0.1 to 12°), with fewer retreatments needed after surgery. Critically, **"no
between-group differences were observed in adjacent untreated or all untreated fingers"** — treating one
finger surgically doesn't appear to protect, or otherwise affect, the fingers left alone. Risk factors
identified for progression or retreatment, regardless of which treatment was used: **younger age at
treatment, smoking, a dominantly-affected proximal interphalangeal joint, and involvement of the little
finger.**
sections.heading: What it found

sections.body:
- **Increase in contracture angle over time**, defined as the trial's specific progression measure, tracked
  separately in treated versus untreated fingers `[¶5]`.
- **Retreatment need**, tracked as a downstream consequence of progression `[¶6]`.

sections.body:
- **DETECT (Dupuytren Treatment Effectiveness Trial)** — the source trial this finger-level analysis draws
  its data from `[¶5]`.
- **Finger-level analysis** — analysing outcomes per finger rather than per patient, which is what lets this
  study separate treated-finger effects from any effect on untreated fingers in the same hand `[¶5]`.

durable results in treated fingers compared with percutaneous methods, although progression and retreatment
rates in untreated fingers are similar across all treatment groups"** — i.e., don't extend the treated-finger
finding to imply any protective effect elsewhere in the hand `[¶7]`. They translate the risk-factor findings
into a specific counseling recommendation: **"Patients at higher risk for progression (ie, young smokers with
affected little fingers) may benefit most from surgery"** `[¶7]`. A funding and conflict-of-interest
disclosure is stated directly: **"The authors have no financial relationships or conflicts of interest to
declare. This study has been funded by the Research Council of Finland"** `[¶7]`.

is a stronger form of the same evidence. **Extends `nocek-2026-recurrence-systematic-review`'s finding that
PIP-joint contractures recur more than MCP-joint ones**: this trial identifies "dominantly affected proximal
interphalangeal joint" as an independent risk factor for progression specifically, naming the same joint as a
risk marker through a different outcome measure (progression angle, not binary recurrence).

sections.body:
**Within about 5 years of an initial procedure, more than 4 in 10 patients needed some further treatment for
Dupuytren's — split roughly into recurrence in the same digit, spread to another digit in the same hand, or
new disease in the opposite hand, each with its own timeline and risk factors** `[¶6]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶5]`

A **single-institution database review**, starting from 658 patients coded for collagenase treatment or
surgical fasciectomy, narrowed to **341 eligible patients** — 141 initially treated with fasciectomy and 200
with collagenase, treated between 2015 and 2019. The primary outcome was simply whether the patient needed
subsequent treatment, and where: the same digit, another digit in the same hand, or the contralateral hand.
sections.heading: Study design

sections.body:
`[¶6]`, `[¶7]`

At a **mean follow-up of 5.3 years, 142 of 341 patients (42%) underwent additional treatment.** That 42%
splits unevenly by location and by timeline: **same-digit revision in 88 patients (26%) at a mean of 3.2
years; another digit in the same hand in 35 patients (10%) at a mean of 3.6 years; and the contralateral hand
in 79 patients (23%) at a mean of 2.3 years** — meaning the opposite hand was, on average, the *fastest* site
to need treatment, even though same-digit recurrence was the single most common outcome. Different factors
predicted each location: **procedure type, multiple digits treated, and initial nontreated contracture**
predicted same-digit retreatment; **younger age, active smoking, and initial nontreated contracture**
predicted spread to another digit in the same hand; and **the dominant hand being the one initially treated,
plus initial nontreated contracture,** predicted treatment later being needed in the other hand.
sections.heading: What it found

sections.body:
- **Recurrence of contracture in the originally treated digit** `[¶6]`.
- **New Dupuytren's intervention needed in a digit that was not initially treated**, whether in the same hand
  or the opposite one `[¶6]`.
- **Pre-existing, untreated contracture in a digit other than the one initially addressed**, named repeatedly
  as a risk factor for further treatment regardless of location `[¶6]`.

- **Contralateral hand** — the hand not initially treated; this study tracks it as a distinct outcome
  location from the treated hand's other digits `[¶4]`.

over 40% likelihood of future intervention for contracture... Key risk factors include age, multiple digits
treated, smoking, and the presence of initially nontreated fingers, which should be incorporated into patient
counseling"** `[¶7]`. The study labels its own evidence tier explicitly: **"3-Retrospective cohort study,
prognostic"** — a lower evidence tier than a randomized trial, stated as such rather than implied `[¶8]`. A
conflict of interest is disclosed directly: **"Dr Blazar is a consultant for Endo Pharmaceuticals"** (a
collagenase manufacturer), with the other authors reporting no related benefits `[¶8]`.

sections.body:
**This is a single-page NHS clinical care pathway, not a narrative source — it specifies exactly which
patients should be referred for surgery, on what criteria, and what happens at every stage from a GP
appointment through to discharge.** `[p.1]`. It is co-branded GIRFT (Getting It Right First Time) and BSSH
(British Society for Surgery of the Hand), dated December 2023, with BAPRAS and the British Orthopaedic
Association also credited.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[p.1]`

The pathway runs Presentation → Referral → Surgical review → Operative procedure → Recovery and
rehabilitation. **Presentation in primary care leads to a specific history-and-examination protocol** (hand
dominance, occupation, interference with daily activities, duration of symptoms, trauma, previous surgery,
recurrence, co-morbidities including diabetes/smoking, and family history) **and a specific examination**
(loss of hand function; skin thickening or pitting in the palm; firm nodules fixed to skin or deep fascia;
fibrous tendon-like cords; flexion deformity of the MCPJs and IPJs; reduced thumb–index webspace; inability
to lay the palm and fingers flat on a table top; and ectopic lesions — nodules over the dorsal PIPJs, soles
of the feet, or penile tissue).

**The pathway names a specific differential diagnosis list to rule out first**: callus, ganglion cyst, giant
cell tumour, inclusion cyst, ulnar nerve palsy, trigger finger, post-trauma or infection, joint disease,
diabetic cheiroarthropathy, camptodactyly, Volkmann's contracture, and (rarely) epithelioid sarcoma.
sections.heading: The five stages

sections.body:
`[p.1]`

**The pathway sets an explicit numeric bar for surgical referral**: "flexion contracture of 30° or more at
the MCPJ or 20° at the PIPJ," or a thumb contracture that impairs function, or previously failed
non-operative management, or rapidly progressive disease. Below that threshold, the pathway branches
differently depending on whether there is diagnostic uncertainty or intolerably painful nodules the primary
clinician isn't trained to inject — either routed to a community MSK service for confirmation and possible
steroid injection, or (if neither applies) simply reassured that "tender nodules [are] likely to become less
tender over time," with cortisone injection offered for pain and radiotherapy noted only as something to
"consider... as part of local audit or research if available" — not a standard offer.
sections.heading: The referral threshold

sections.body:
`[p.1]`

Once referred, the pathway requires **assessment by, or supervised by, a surgeon with appropriate training
in Hand Surgery**, confirmation of diagnosis, and a formal informed-consent process, before choice of
procedure — **percutaneous fasciotomy in outpatients, or listing for daycase surgery** — based on surgeon
preference, patient factors, and disease characteristics.

Recovery is staged explicitly: **at 3–5 days post-surgery**, dressing changes, wound checks, range-of-motion
exercises and a night splint are considered; **at 10–14 days**, suture removal (if needed) and ongoing hand
therapy, splinting, and scar management, with one review by the surgeon or an Extended Scope Practitioner.
The pathway's endpoint is **"Discharge with Patient Initiated Follow-up (PIFU)"** — the patient, not a
scheduled appointment, triggers any further contact.
sections.heading: Surgical review, procedure, and recovery

sections.body:
- **Firm nodules fixed to the skin or deep fascia, with skin thickening or pitting in the palm** `[p.1]`.
- **Fibrous, tendon-like cords, and flexion deformity at the MCPJ and IPJ** `[p.1]`.
- **Reduced span between thumb and index finger webspace; inability to lay the palm flat on a table** `[p.1]`.
- **Ectopic nodules over the dorsal PIPJs, soles of the feet, or penile tissue** `[p.1]`.
- **Persistent painful nodules**, distinguished in the pathway from nodules that are simply present but not
  painful `[p.1]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **MCPJ / PIPJ** — metacarpophalangeal joint / proximal interphalangeal joint, the two joint locations the
  pathway's surgical threshold is defined against `[p.1]`.
- **Patient Initiated Follow-up (PIFU)** — a discharge model where the patient contacts the service if
  needed, rather than being given a routine follow-up appointment `[p.1]`.

sections.body:
**Dupuytren's is framed here not just as a hand condition but as an unusually convenient model for fibrosis
in general — because the diseased tissue is easy to reach and sample, it can teach researchers about fibrotic
diseases elsewhere in the body that are much harder to study directly** `[¶4]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶4]`

The review states its own scope directly: **"We review the biology of Dupuytren's disease (DD), a common
localised fibrotic disorder of the hand."** Three factors are named as jointly driving disease development:
**genetic and environmental factors, and epigenetic signalling** — not any one of these alone. At the tissue
level, **"the early-stage disease nodules comprise a complex milieu of stromal and immune cells which
interact to promote disease development"** — the nodule is described as an active site of cell-to-cell
interaction, not simply a lump of thickened tissue.
sections.heading: What the review covers

sections.body:
`[¶4]`

The review flags one finding as clinically notable: **"Recently, inhibition of tumour necrosis factor (TNF)
locally resulted in softening and a decrease in nodule size, potentially controlling disease progression."**
It's stated as a potential mechanism worth pursuing, not an established treatment — the review doesn't claim
this translates into a proven therapy at this stage.
sections.heading: A specific treatment lead

sections.body:
`[¶4]`

**"Unlike fibrotic disorders of the visceral organs, the easy access to tissue in DD patients enables
dissection of the cellular landscape and molecular signalling pathways."** The review's stated payoff is
explicitly two-directional: understanding Dupuytren's better, and using Dupuytren's as a window into **"less-
accessible fibrotic tissues"** elsewhere in the body.
sections.heading: Why the review frames this as broader than one disease

sections.body:
Not directly addressed — this is a cell-biology and molecular-mechanism review, not a clinical-presentation
source. Its material is about what is happening inside a nodule, not what a patient notices.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **TNF (tumour necrosis factor)** — the specific inflammatory signalling molecule this review names as a
  local drug target with an early positive result `[¶4]`.
- **Stromal-immune cell milieu** — this review's term for the mixed cell population inside an early nodule
  that it says interacts to drive disease development `[¶4]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- **Dupuytren's as an "accessible" fibrotic disorder** — the review's own framing device, contrasting easily
  sampled hand tissue against fibrosis in organs that can't be biopsied nearly as readily `[¶4]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
The TNF-inhibition finding is stated carefully as directional, not proven: **"resulted in softening and a
decrease in nodule size, potentially controlling disease progression"** — "potentially" is the review's own
word, not an inserted hedge. No conflicts of interest are declared: **"No interests are declared"** `[¶4]`.

**No direct conflict with the clinical-treatment sources in this library** (`shaheen-2025-treatment-comparison-review`,

fasciotomy, and collagenase for already-formed cords, while this review's TNF-inhibition finding targets
early nodules before a cord has formed, a different disease stage entirely. **Relevant to
`sayadi-2019-molecular-pathogenesis-review`**, another basic-science review of the same disease — worth
comparing once both are in the library for where their accounts of genetic/molecular drivers agree or differ.

sections.body:
**NICE's headline verdict is a qualified yes: "current evidence on the safety and efficacy of needle
fasciotomy for Dupuytren's contracture appears adequate to support the use of the procedure, provided that
normal arrangements are in place for consent, audit and clinical governance"** `[¶1]`. It is framed as a
routine procedure, not one requiring the special research-and-audit safeguards NICE attaches to radiotherapy
for the same condition.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶2]`

**"Needle fasciotomy is an outpatient procedure in which one or more fibrous bands (contractures) are
divided using a blade or the bevel of a needle,"** performed in either the palm or the fingers. The guidance
is explicit that this treats the symptom, not the disease: **"Treatment seeks to restore hand function and
prevent progression, because the underlying disease will remain."** Data on non-surgical alternatives is
described as absent: **"Data are lacking on the effectiveness of most non-surgical treatments for
Dupuytren's contracture, such as vitamin E cream and ultrasonic therapy."**
sections.heading: What the procedure is, and what it doesn't do

sections.body:
`[¶2]`

**"The main benefit offered by this procedure is a short-term reduction in the degree of contracture."**
NICE gives a specific recurrence figure: **"Recurrence rate is approximately 50% at 3 to 5 years and seems
to depend on the severity of the disease."** Patient selection matters — **"individuals with less severe
disease and/or with metacarpophalangeal joint contracture benefited most from this procedure"** — and a
Specialist Adviser is quoted directly on the tradeoff against open surgery: **"although the procedure was
not as efficacious in the long term as open surgery, patients experienced less morbidity and had faster
recovery."** The guidance frames it as particularly suited to a specific patient group: **"the procedure was
considered particularly suitable for older patients who are unsuitable for more major surgery"** — and,
because it "can be repeated," recurrence doesn't foreclose future treatment.
sections.heading: Efficacy, recurrence, and who benefits most

sections.body:
`[¶2]`

Two sources of complication data are cited without being merged into one figure: **"Common complications
reported in the studies included splitting of the skin, localised pain and nerve injuries,"** while
**Specialist Advisers separately listed nerve injury, tendon injury and infection as the main complications,
with one Advisor citing a complication rate of 1% or less.**
sections.heading: Complications

sections.body:
- **Difficulty extending the fingers, from a fibrous cord in the palm or finger** `[¶2]`.
- **Recurrence of contracture after treatment** — described as expected in roughly half of patients within
  3 to 5 years, not a sign the procedure failed outright `[¶2]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Needle fasciotomy (needle aponeurotomy)** — dividing, not removing, a Dupuytren's cord with a needle
  bevel `[¶2]`.
- **Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint** — the joint location NICE specifically flags as predicting a better
  outcome from this procedure `[¶2]`.

sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
NICE states this recommendation is conditional, not absolute: it holds only **"provided that normal
arrangements are in place for consent, audit and clinical governance"** `[¶1]` — a lighter condition than the
"special arrangements" NICE attaches to radiotherapy for the same disease. The ~50%-at-3-to-5-years
recurrence figure is stated as a real limitation, not smoothed over, and the guidance is explicit that data
on non-surgical alternatives (vitamin E cream, ultrasonic therapy) simply doesn't exist rather than showing
those options don't work `[¶2]`.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Converges directly with `nocek-2026-recurrence-systematic-review`**, which independently quantifies needle
aponeurotomy's recurrence at 46.4% over a mean 3.8-year follow-up — close to, if somewhat higher than, this
guidance's "approximately 50% at 3 to 5 years," and consistent with the same conclusion that needle-based
treatment recurs more than surgery. **Also relevant to `girft-bssh-dupuytrens-pathway`**, which lists
percutaneous fasciotomy as one of its two surgical-review pathways without stating a recurrence figure of its
own — this guidance supplies the number that pathway leaves implicit.

sections.body:
**NICE's verdict is conditional and cautious: radiotherapy "raises no major safety concerns," but efficacy
evidence is "inadequate in quantity and quality" and "difficult to interpret because of uncertainty about
the natural history of Dupuytren's disease" — so the procedure "should only be used with special
arrangements for clinical governance, consent and audit or research"** `[¶1]`. This is a materially more
cautious stance than NICE takes on needle fasciotomy for the same disease.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶2]`

NICE is explicit that there's no formal line: **"There is no formal clinical definition of early disease but
the term is generally used for patients with contractures of 30 degrees or less, with or without palmar
disease."** The guidance also states plainly that **"not all patients have progressive disease, and the
natural history of the disease is not well understood"** — the same uncertainty that limits how confidently
efficacy can be judged. The stated aim of radiotherapy is **"to prevent or postpone disease progression, and
reduce the need for surgical intervention,"** with a mechanism that is itself uncertain: **"thought to affect
the development and growth rate of fibroblasts in the palmar fascia"** `[¶3]`.
sections.heading: What "early disease" means

sections.body:
`[¶6]`, `[¶8]`, `[¶10]`, `[¶12]`

Four separate patient groups supply the efficacy evidence, and NICE keeps their numbers distinct rather than
pooling them:

| Cohort | Dose | Follow-up | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| RCT, 129 patients / 198 hands | 30 Gy vs 21 Gy | 1 year | Regression in 56% (30 Gy) / 53% (21 Gy) of hands (objective assessment); stable in a further 37%/38%; overall progression 8% |
| Case series, 206 patients | 32 Gy | median 40 months | Regression in 45% (93/206); no further progression in 80% |
| Case series, 135 patients / 208 hands | 30 Gy | median 13 years | Regression in 10% of hands, stable in 59%, progression in 31% |
| Case series, 33 patients / 60 sites | (dose not stated in this excerpt) | median 31 months | Progression at any location in 61% of patients; in-field progression 23% of sites, with 4 sites successfully re-irradiated |

**The 13-year cohort's own patient-reported relief breakdown is worth keeping distinct from the "regression"
figure above**: complete relief in 16%, good relief in 18%, minor relief in 32%, unchanged in 14%, and
progression of symptoms in 20% of patients `[¶10]`. Subsequent surgery was needed in 3% of the RCT patients
within 1 year, 20% of the 13-year cohort's hands, and 6% of the 33-patient cohort within 31 months `[¶14]`.
Patient satisfaction, where measured, was high: a mean 7.9±2.7 out of 10 in the 206-patient cohort, and 94%
of the 33-patient cohort considered the treatment successful `[¶16]`.
sections.heading: Efficacy, across four cohorts

sections.body:
`[¶24]`–`[¶53]`

**Acute effects** (within about 4 weeks) reported across the cohorts include skin tenderness, redness,
peeling, or mild pain (50% in a 17-patient cohort); dry skin or redness (38% of hands in the RCT); dry
desquamation (5% of hands) and wet desquamation (2%); extensive erythema (6% of hands in the RCT, 20% of
patients in the 206-patient cohort); and pronounced swelling (2% of hands).

**Chronic effects** reported include mild tightness, dryness, skin thickening, mild swelling, and decreased
sensation (31% of the 17-patient cohort at a mean 35 months); skin dryness, increased desquamation, mild
atrophy or slight subcutaneous fibrosis needing topical treatment (16% of hands at 30 Gy and 11% at 21 Gy
within 3 months, falling to 4–5% by 12 months, in the RCT); lack of sweating (4% of the 206-patient cohort);
skin atrophy and telangiectasia (3% each in the 206-patient cohort; mild atrophy with occasional
telangiectasia in 7% of the 13-year cohort's hands); altered heat/pain sensation (4% of RCT hands); and, in
the 33-patient/60-site cohort specifically, subjective weakness (3% of sites), reduced nail health (3%), and
hyperpigmentation (3%).

**No radiation-induced malignancy was reported in the literature NICE reviewed**, despite specialist advisers
naming it as a theoretical (not observed) risk alongside poor wound healing from surgery on irradiated skin
`[¶55]`.
sections.heading: Safety — acute and chronic toxicity

sections.body:
- **Regression, stabilisation, or progression of existing nodules and cords, tracked as the three primary
  outcome categories across every cohort in this guidance** `[¶6]`, `[¶10]`.
- **New nodules, new cords, or increased flexion deformity as markers of on-treatment progression** — 6%,
  4%, and 6% of hands respectively in the RCT `[¶6]`.
- **Post-treatment skin symptoms**: tenderness, dryness, thickening, reduced sweating, altered sensation, or
  weakness at the treated site `[¶24]`–`[¶49]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Gy (Gray)** — the radiation dose unit this guidance's cohorts are grouped by (21, 30, or 32 Gy) `[¶6]`.
- **Acute versus chronic toxicity** — NICE's own split for organizing side-effect data, roughly at the
  4-week mark `[¶21]`, `[¶35]`.
- **In-field versus out-of-field progression** — whether the disease worsens inside the area that was
  actually irradiated, or elsewhere `[¶12]`.

sections.body:
This is the most explicitly hedged source in the library so far. NICE states directly that the efficacy
evidence is **"inadequate in quantity and quality"** and that interpreting it is complicated by not knowing
**"the natural history of Dupuytren's disease"** in the first place `[¶1]` — meaning even a genuine
"regression" rate can't cleanly be separated from cases that might have improved on their own. The committee
also flagged, without resolving, a structural problem: **"despite the recommendations in the previous
guidance for audit, and encouragement for further research, data collection since the guidance was published
had been disappointing"** `[¶58]`. That combination — real numbers, explicitly stated as too weak to found a
confident recommendation on — is the reason this guidance lands on "special arrangements for governance,
consent and audit," not a routine recommendation.

"consider... as part of local audit or research if available" rather than a standard offer — the same
caution this guidance's own evidence grading explains in detail. **No sources yet in this library report a
recurrence figure specifically for radiotherapy comparable to the treatment-recurrence figures
`nocek-2026-recurrence-systematic-review` gives for LF/CCH/NA** — radiotherapy targets early, pre-cord
disease and isn't directly comparable to those cord-release procedures, and this library has no source yet
that states that distinction explicitly.

sections.body:
**Across ten prospective studies and nearly 1,700 treated joints, recurrence after Dupuytren treatment was
common regardless of method — but the three treatments recur at very different rates: limited fasciectomy
16.5%, collagenase 32.5%, needle aponeurotomy 46.4%** `[¶7]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶5]`

The review is deliberately restricted to studies that could actually answer the recurrence question
cleanly: **"prospective cohort series or randomized controlled trials treating DC with LF, CCH, and/or NA,"**
requiring **"≥2-year, in-person clinical follow-up and explicit definition of contracture recurrence."**
Studies relying on telephone or questionnaire-only follow-up, non-English publications, studies with no
recurrence data at follow-up, or fewer than 15 patients were excluded — a deliberate filter against the
weaker data other reviews sometimes include.
sections.heading: How the evidence was screened

sections.body:
`[¶6]`, `[¶7]`

**Ten studies, 1,411 patients, 1,698 treated joints, mean follow-up 3.8 years.** Across studies, **"LF
demonstrated a lower risk of recurrence than both CCH and NA, and CCH demonstrated a lower risk of recurrence
than NA"** — the same ordering restated with hard numbers in the conclusion: **LF 16.5%, CCH 32.5% (an
"intermediate" position), NA 46.4% (the highest)**. **Joint location also mattered independently of
treatment**: **"Recurrence was less likely in the treatment of MCP versus PIP contractures across all
treatments,"** and this held regardless of which of the three treatments was used. Reintervention followed
the same pattern as recurrence — **"a lower likelihood of reinterventions after LF than after CCH or NA"** —
and **commonly reported complications were digital nerve injury, tendon injury, skin tears, swelling, pain,
and bleeding** `[¶6]`.
sections.heading: What it found

sections.body:
- **Recurrence of contracture after initial successful treatment**, defined explicitly per study rather than
  left to inconsistent wording `[¶5]`.
- **Need for a repeat procedure (reintervention)** as a distinct, trackable consequence of recurrence `[¶6]`.
- **Digital nerve injury, tendon injury, skin tears, swelling, pain, and bleeding** as the complications
  reported across the pooled studies `[¶6]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Needle aponeurotomy (NA)** — this review's term for the same procedure `nice-htg21-needle-fasciotomy`
  calls needle fasciotomy `[¶4]`.
- **MCP versus PIP joint** — the two joint locations whose recurrence risk this review compares directly,
  independent of which treatment was used `[¶6]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body: None — figures are given as direct percentages and relative comparisons.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
The review's own clinical-relevance framing resists a simple "LF is best" reading: **"LF offers greater
durability and a lower likelihood of subsequent procedures than CCH or NA... however, the clinician must also
weigh the length of recovery and potential complications between these three treatment options"** `[¶8]`. It
also flags a specific sub-group caution: **"Patients with PIP contractures should be counseled about a higher
recurrence risk and potential need for closer follow-up"** regardless of which treatment they choose `[¶8]`.
A conflict-of-interest statement is disclosed directly in the source rather than omitted: **"Dr. Mark A.
Vitale served on the advisory board for Endo Pharmaceuticals, Inc in 2022"** — Endo being a manufacturer with
a commercial interest in collagenase — **"the other authors have no relevant conflicts to disclose"** `[¶8]`.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Converges tightly with `shaheen-2025-treatment-comparison-review`**, which reaches the identical ordering
(LF most durable, then CCH, then needle-based treatment least durable) via relative risk rather than raw
percentages — two independent systematic reviews landing on the same ranking. **Converges with
`nice-htg21-needle-fasciotomy`**, whose ~50%-at-3-to-5-years figure for needle fasciotomy sits close to this
review's 46.4% at a mean 3.8 years for the same procedure under a different name (needle aponeurotomy).
**Relevant to `detect-2026-progression-rct`**, which finds surgery outperforms needle fasciotomy and
collagenase on progression within treated fingers specifically — consistent in direction, though that trial
measures progression of contracture angle rather than binary recurrence.

sections.body:
**This source is a paraphrased summary of a Reddit comment thread (see the source file's own header note),
not a verbatim capture of it.** Across the thread, patients and family members describe genetics-linked
family clustering, disagree with each other about alcohol and hand-use as risk factors, and report mostly
discouraging, recurrence-heavy treatment experiences, alongside one detailed clinical explanation of the
collagenase procedure from a self-identified hand surgeon `[¶1]`, `[¶2]`, `[¶3]`. Every claim below is
anecdotal — a commenter's own account, not established fact.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶2]`

Several commenters described the condition running in their families, including one account of a father and
older brother both affected, the father having had surgery on both hands. Multiple commenters connected the
condition to Northern European ancestry, including references to "Viking disease" and to a link with
Neanderthal ancestry that one commenter said they'd read about — self-reported framing, not sourced to any
study in the thread itself.
sections.heading: Family clustering and ancestry

sections.body:
`[¶3]`

Commenters did not agree with each other. Some linked the condition to heavy alcohol use; at least two
commenters said they had the condition despite little or no alcohol use, one adding they had worked in the
trades their whole life. Hand use itself was similarly disputed — some described years of manual labor before
onset, while one commenter said they'd seen a video claiming the opposite, that the condition is worse in
people who do *not* use their hands for manual work. **The thread does not resolve either disagreement** —
it's presented here as exactly that, an open disagreement among patients, not a finding.
sections.heading: Disagreement over causes

sections.body:
`[¶4]`, `[¶5]`

Reported outcomes were mixed and skewed toward disappointing: one commenter's surgery was followed by
recurrence "worse than ever" after 40+ stitches and months of therapy; another reported a family member's
day-surgery with no recurrence since; one commenter who'd had both an enzyme-injection treatment and surgery
on both hands said they'd choose surgery again over repeating the injection, and that a since-unstraightened
finger was from treatment scar tissue rather than a returned contracture. **The self-identified hand surgeon
in the thread was direct about the underlying limitation**: none of the treatment options cure the disease,
and recurrence is typical if a patient lives long enough after treatment. That same commenter explained the
collagenase (Xiaflex) procedure clinically: the joint must be contracted to at least 20 degrees to qualify,
the patient returns 48–72 hours after injection for manual cord-breaking, and the hand is numbed beforehand.
sections.heading: Treatment experience

sections.body:
`[¶6]`

One commenter suggested radiation therapy as a treatment more established in Europe than in the US, prompting
interest from the original poster (who has the condition) in seeking it out if no US option worked for them.
Other commenters pointed to further patient-community resources — a dedicated Dupuytren's-focused subreddit,
and a community guide referenced only by title, not summarized in the thread itself `[¶7]`.
sections.heading: What the thread flagged as missing or worth knowing

sections.body:
- **Recurrence of contracture after surgery or injection treatment**, described by multiple commenters as the
  dominant experience rather than the exception `[¶4]`.
- **A finger that no longer straightens due to scar tissue from treatment**, distinguished by one commenter
  from a genuinely returned contracture `[¶4]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Xiaflex** — the brand name one commenter (a self-identified hand surgeon) used for the collagenase
  injection procedure, matching the "collagenase" treatment named in this library's clinical sources `[¶5]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- **"Viking disease"** — the informal nickname multiple commenters used for the condition's association with
  Northern European ancestry `[¶2]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
This entire source is anecdotal by design — it is patient and family self-report, not clinical evidence, and
is tagged `patient_experience` / `anecdotal` for exactly that reason. Where the thread itself contains
disagreement (alcohol, hand-use as causes), that disagreement is preserved here rather than resolved one way,
because the thread doesn't resolve it either.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Converges with the clinical sources on recurrence being common**: `nocek-2026-recurrence-systematic-review`,
`shaheen-2025-treatment-comparison-review`, and `nice-htg21-needle-fasciotomy` all report substantial
recurrence rates across treatments, consistent with this thread's mostly-discouraging patient-reported
outcomes. **Converges with `girft-bssh-dupuytrens-pathway` and `nice-htg427-radiotherapy`** on radiation
therapy being a real but non-standard option, more established outside the US — the commenter's impression
matches what the clinical guidance itself states. **No clinical source in this library supports or refutes**
the alcohol-versus-no-alcohol or hand-use-versus-no-hand-use disagreement raised here — it remains an open
question in this library specifically because no source yet addresses it directly.

sections.body:
**This is a systematic review of the basic-science (not clinical-treatment) literature on Dupuytren's,
organizing 77 included studies into molecular, structural, and genetic categories, with the explicit goal of
pointing toward future biologic treatments that target the disease process rather than just cutting or
dissolving the resulting cord** `[¶7]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶4]`

The review opens from an existing staging framework: **"Ever since the classification of Dupuytren disease
into the proliferative, involutional, and residual stages, extensive research has been performed to uncover
the molecular underpinnings of the disease."** Its stated goal is two-part — **"to systematically review the
basic science literature pertaining to Dupuytren disease and suggest a new approach to treatment"** — meaning
this source is explicitly reaching beyond a pure literature summary toward a treatment proposal.
sections.heading: Framing and scope

sections.body:
`[¶5]`, `[¶6]`

The review followed **PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis)
guidelines**, searching MEDLINE for basic-science literature falling into one or more of three categories:
**"(1) Molecular alterations, (2) Structural alterations, and (3) Genetic predisposition."** Of **177
articles screened, 77 met inclusion criteria** and were sorted into those three categories for the review's
body.
sections.heading: Method and yield

sections.body:
`[¶7]`

**"The pathophysiological changes involved in Dupuytren's disease can be divided into a number of molecular
and structural alterations with genetic predisposition playing a contributory role."** The review's stated
payoff for this categorization is treatment-directed: **"Understanding these changes can allow for the
development of biologics which may disrupt and halt the disease process"** — a research direction, not a
treatment that exists yet.
sections.heading: Conclusion

sections.body:
Not directly addressed — like `layton-2023-fibrotic-disorder-review`, this is a mechanism-level review rather
than a clinical-presentation source.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Proliferative, involutional, and residual stages** — the disease-staging framework this review says
  motivated the underlying research it's summarizing `[¶4]`.
- **PRISMA** — the reporting standard this systematic review followed for how studies were searched and
  screened `[¶5]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
None — this source reports its method and findings in review-methodology language rather than illustrative
comparisons.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
The review is explicit about its own screening funnel (177 screened, 77 included), which lets a reader judge
how selective it was, rather than simply asserting a conclusion `[¶6]`. Its forward-looking claim about
biologics is stated as a possibility opened up by the science, not a therapy already validated: **"may
disrupt and halt the disease process,"** not "does" `[¶7]`.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**No direct conflict with `layton-2023-fibrotic-disorder-review`** — both are basic-science reviews of the
same disease reaching the same general shape of conclusion (multiple molecular/structural drivers, genetics
playing a contributory rather than sole role), though this review is broader in scope (77 studies across
three categories) while Layton's is narrower and more recent, with a specific, named drug target (TNF) this
review's available excerpt doesn't mention by name. **No conflict with the clinical-treatment sources** in
this library — this review's territory (why the disease happens at a cellular level) doesn't overlap with
their territory (which existing procedure works best on an already-formed cord).

sections.body:
**No treatment wins outright: PNF, CCH, and LF reduce contracture by a similar amount long-term, but LF holds
that reduction better at the cost of a higher risk of rare serious complications** `[¶4]`. The review states
its own motivation directly: **"There is currently no consensus on the optimal treatment for Dupuytren
contracture. Prior meta-analyses have been limited by suboptimal data synthesis methodologies."**
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶4]`

Built from **17 publications and 1,010 patients**, comparing PNF, CCH, and LF against outcomes at 3 months, 1
year, and 2 to 3 years — residual contracture, recurrence rate, hand function, pain, global satisfaction, and
adverse events. On long-term contracture reduction, the review found **"no clinically important difference"**
between treatments, graded high-to-moderate certainty: PNF versus LF, mean difference 7.6° (95% CI 1.8 to
13.4°); CCH versus LF, mean difference 4.8° (95% CI −1.3 to 10.9°). But recurrence and safety diverge sharply:
**LF carries the lowest long-term recurrence risk** (PNF versus LF relative risk 12.3, 95% CI 1.6 to 92.4; CCH
versus LF relative risk 9.5, 95% CI 1.2 to 73.4) — while **LF also carries a higher risk of serious adverse
events than PNF** (relative risk 0.5, 95% CI 0.3 to 0.9), and **CCH carries a higher risk of overall adverse
events than PNF** (relative risk 4.8, 95% CI 2.9 to 7.0).
sections.heading: The evidence base and what it found

sections.body:
- **Residual contracture angle after treatment**, tracked separately from whether the contracture later
  returns `[¶4]`.
- **Recurrence of contracture** as its own outcome, distinct from initial correction `[¶4]`.
- **Pain, hand function, and global satisfaction** named as outcomes the review tracked, though the specific
  figures for these were not given in the excerpt available here `[¶4]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **GRADE approach** — the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation framework used
  to rate how certain each finding is `[¶4]`.
- **PNF / CCH / LF** — percutaneous needle fasciotomy, collagenase clostridium histolyticum injection, and
  limited fasciectomy — the three treatments compared throughout `[¶4]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
None — this is a quantitative meta-analysis reported in effect sizes and confidence intervals, not
illustrative language.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
The review itself grades its findings by certainty rather than stating them all at one confidence level: the
"no important difference in contracture reduction" finding is **"high- to moderate-certainty evidence,"**
while the recurrence and durability findings are explicitly **"moderate-certainty evidence"** `[¶4]`. The
authors' own conclusion resists a single "best" answer: **"CCH, PNF, and LF are equally effective in
long-term contracture reduction. However, LF yields more durable results at a higher risk of rare but serious
adverse events... ultimate treatment decisions should be tailored to individual patient preferences"**
`[¶4]`.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Converges closely with `nocek-2026-recurrence-systematic-review`**, which independently quantifies the same
recurrence ordering with hard percentages (LF 16.5%, CCH 32.5%, NA 46.4%) rather than this review's relative
risks — the two sources reinforce each other on which treatment recurs least, from different meta-analytic
methods. **Also converges with `nice-htg21-needle-fasciotomy`**, whose stated ~50%-at-3-to-5-years recurrence
figure for needle fasciotomy sits consistently above collagenase and well above the low end this review
implies for LF. **Relevant to `detect-2026-progression-rct`**, a single RCT (not included in this review,
published after it) that reaches a similar directional conclusion — surgery more durable than the
percutaneous options — from primary trial data rather than pooled studies.

sections.body:
**This is a paraphrased summary of comments under an educational Dupuytren's video, not a verbatim capture —
see the source file's header.** The comments are dominated by two things: mostly negative or mixed
self-reported treatment outcomes, and a cluster of self-treatment remedies (boron, hormone replacement
therapy, manual stretching, a fasting/supplement combination, ice water) that individual commenters reported
trying, several of which drew explicit pushback from other commenters in the same thread `[¶2]`, `[¶5]`,
`[¶6]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶2]`, `[¶3]`, `[¶4]`

Surgical outcomes skewed negative: one commenter reported four surgeries with recurrence every time, and
described physical therapy (in their experience) as making things come back "faster and often worse"; another
said surgery left both treated fingers worse, with ongoing pain months into physiotherapy. On collagenase
(Xiaflex), one commenter reported it working well in one hand but having no effect at all on a repeat
injection in the other hand, describing themselves as having become "immune" to it, and was scheduled for a
minimally invasive procedure to remove the cord instead. **Multiple commenters directly disputed that the
condition is painless**, with one describing significant ongoing pain despite injections and surgery, and
another confirming in reply that it can be very painful.
sections.heading: Treatment outcomes reported

sections.body:
`[¶5]`, `[¶6]`

**Boron** drew the most discussion: one commenter reported their spouse's contracture — which had returned
after both surgery and injections — resolving over a few months on a daily boron regimen. This drew explicit
pushback in the replies: one commenter stated there is no direct scientific evidence or clinical literature
supporting boron as a Dupuytren's treatment (while noting boron is used for arthritis-related inflammation);
another questioned whether the improvement actually followed the earlier surgery rather than the boron
itself; several asked for exact dosing without a clear answer settled in the thread. **Other remedies were
each raised by a single commenter, without supporting evidence cited**: hormone replacement therapy (one
commenter linked resolution of both their Dupuytren's and general joint pain to starting HRT at 59, no
recurrence four years on); regular manual stretching of the fingers (one commenter reported more range of
motion and a smaller nodule over time, while separately noting skepticism that the video itself promotes an
injectable-enzyme treatment); a combination of intermittent fasting, daily olive oil, and NAC supplementation
(one commenter reported reduced burning sensation and apparent improvement, explicitly framed their own
account as uncertain which element helped, and invited others to try it and report back); and holding the
hand in ice water for twenty minutes (raised as an open question, with no one in the thread reporting having
tried it).
sections.heading: The unverified remedies, and how the thread treated them

sections.body:
`[¶7]`

One commenter proposed, as their own theory rather than a cited medical claim, that their condition traced
back to a specific childhood finger injury that healed poorly, framing Dupuytren's-like tissue as the body
forming hardened "callus" in response to repeated strain on already-damaged tissue — extending the same
explanation to an unrelated old toe injury, and cautioning other commenters against overexerting their hands
on that basis.
sections.heading: A patient's own causal theory

sections.body:
`[¶8]`

One commenter argued the video omitted radiation therapy, describing it as common outside the United States
and increasingly available domestically — the same point a commenter raised independently in the Reddit
thread in this library.
sections.heading: What the video was said to be missing

sections.body:
- **Pain, disputed as present or absent** — several commenters directly contradicted the framing that
  Dupuytren's is typically painless `[¶4]`.
- **Recurrence after surgery, and reduced or absent response to a repeat collagenase injection** `[¶2]`,
  `[¶3]`.
- **Reduced range of motion and nodule size**, reported by one commenter as improving with regular manual
  stretching — a single, unverified account `[¶6]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Xiaflex** — the same collagenase brand name used by the commenter in `reddit-til-dupuytrens-thread`,
  consistent with this library's clinical sources' use of "collagenase" `[¶3]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body: None distinct from `reddit-til-dupuytrens-thread`'s "Viking" framing, which also recurs here.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
**Every remedy in this note beyond surgery and collagenase is a single commenter's unverified account**, and
is presented that way deliberately — this note does not imply boron, HRT, stretching, fasting/NAC, or ice
water are effective treatments, only that individual viewers reported trying them, with the boron account
specifically challenged within the same comment thread by other commenters citing an absence of clinical
evidence `[¶5]`.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Converges with `reddit-til-dupuytrens-thread`** on painful, recurrence-heavy patient experience, and on
radiation therapy being an overlooked option — two independent patient-community sources landing on the same
observations. **No clinical source in this library supports boron, HRT, manual stretching, fasting/NAC, or
ice water as Dupuytren's treatments** — these appear only in this note and in `reddit-til-dupuytrens-thread`
(HRT and stretching do not appear there), and should not be cited elsewhere in this library as anything more
than a self-reported anecdote.
